nodes.label: Alexander conquest
nodes.full: Alexander's forces absorbed Judea into his empire with little recorded resistance following the siege of Tyre and Gaza — a later Jewish tradition preserved only in Josephus, writing more than three centuries afterward, describes Alexander personally visiting Jerusalem and paying homage to the high priest, a vivid story almost universally regarded by modern historians as legendary embellishment rather than a historical event, absent from any earlier or independent source.
nodes.src: Josephus, Antiquities 11.8.5, on Alexander's alleged Jerusalem visit, widely treated as apocryphal; compare the far better attested sieges of Tyre and Gaza during the same 332 BC campaign.

nodes.label: Ptolemaic century
nodes.full: After Alexander's empire fragmented among his generals, Judea fell to Ptolemaic Egypt following the Wars of the Diadochi and remained a comparatively quiet frontier province for roughly a century, governed through the high priesthood with substantial local autonomy in religious and civil law in exchange for tribute — a stable arrangement that lasted until Seleucid Syria finally wrested the region away by force.
nodes.src: Ptolemaic administration of Coele-Syria (including Judea), 301–200 BC, following the Third Diadoch War's settlement.

nodes.label: Panion
nodes.full: Antiochus III's decisive victory over Ptolemaic forces at Panion transferred Judea permanently to Seleucid control, and the new regime initially confirmed Jerusalem's traditional privileges and tax exemptions in gratitude for the city's cooperation — a favourable start to Seleucid rule that would curdle within a generation under Antiochus III's son.
nodes.src: Battle of Panion (Panium), 200 BC; Josephus, Antiquities 12.3.3, on Antiochus III's initial privileges granted to Jerusalem.

nodes.label: Antiochus IV persecution
nodes.full: Antiochus IV Epiphanes outlawed Sabbath observance, circumcision and Jewish dietary law on pain of death and installed an altar to Olympian Zeus within the Jerusalem Temple itself — whether primarily religious zealotry, a response to internal Jewish factional politics over the high priesthood, or an attempt to forcibly integrate a troublesome province remains debated, but the decree's severity made armed resistance, rather than accommodation, the response of a significant part of the Judean population.
nodes.src: 1 Maccabees 1:41–64; 2 Maccabees 6:1–11.

nodes.label: Mattathias at Modein
nodes.full: When a royal officer ordered the elderly priest Mattathias to offer a pagan sacrifice at Modein, he refused, killed both a compliant Jew who stepped forward to comply and the officer himself, tore down the altar, and fled to the hills with his five sons calling on "everyone who is zealous for the law" to follow — a single act of defiance the text presents as the spark igniting the entire revolt.
nodes.src: 1 Maccabees 2:1–28.

nodes.label: Resurrection hope amid martyrdom
nodes.full: A vivid narrative of a mother and her seven sons tortured to death in succession for refusing to eat pork rather than violate Jewish law includes some of the clearest early expressions of a hope for individual bodily resurrection in Jewish literature, with several sons explicitly telling their executioners that God would restore the very bodies being destroyed — theological language that would go on to shape later Jewish and Christian thought about martyrdom and resurrection alike.
nodes.src: 2 Maccabees 7:1–42, especially verses 9, 11, 14 and 23 on bodily resurrection.

nodes.label: Mother and seven sons
nodes.full: Forced to watch her sons tortured and killed one by one for refusing to break Jewish dietary law, a mother whom later tradition would name Hannah encouraged each of them in turn to accept death rather than apostasy before she herself was killed last — one of the most sustained and personally focused narratives of individual resistance and family loss to survive from the entire Hellenistic-era Jewish world, however much its precise details reflect later literary shaping.
nodes.src: 2 Maccabees 7:1–42.

nodes.label: Judah Maccabee campaigns
nodes.full: Mattathias's son Judah, nicknamed "the Hammer" (Maccabee), won a string of victories against Seleucid forces at Beth Horon, Emmaus and Beth Zur using guerrilla tactics against a numerically superior professional army, recaptured Jerusalem and rededicated the Temple in 164 BC, and was ultimately killed in battle at Elasa in 160 BC against a renewed Seleucid offensive — his death did not end the revolt, which his brothers Jonathan and Simon carried on to eventual full independence.
nodes.src: 1 Maccabees 3:1–9:22.

nodes.label: Temple rededication
nodes.full: Judah Maccabee's forces cleansed and rededicated the defiled Temple exactly three years after Antiochus IV's altar to Zeus had been installed there, relighting the menorah in a ceremony the text says lasted eight days — the historical origin of the festival of Hanukkah, commemorating not a military victory directly but the specific restoration of undefiled worship.
nodes.src: 1 Maccabees 4:36–59; 2 Maccabees 10:1–8.

nodes.label: Treaty with Rome
nodes.full: Judah Maccabee sent envoys to Rome shortly before his death to secure a formal treaty of friendship and mutual defence against the Seleucids — the first direct Judean-Roman diplomatic relationship, struck while Rome was still a distant potential counterweight rather than a threat, a striking irony given that the same power invoked here as an ally against Seleucid domination would end Hasmonean independence entirely within little more than a century.
nodes.src: 1 Maccabees 8:1–32, on the embassy and treaty terms, 161 BC.

nodes.label: 1 and 2 Maccabees
nodes.full: 1 Maccabees, a sober near-contemporary military and political history, and 2 Maccabees, a more theologically driven and vividly dramatic account, were both composed within a century or so of the events they describe, yet neither was included in the Hebrew Bible's eventual canon — both survive instead through the Greek Septuagint and remain canonical scripture in Catholic and Orthodox Christian traditions while holding a valued but non-scriptural historical status in Judaism, a striking divergence in how the same founding national narrative was preserved by different religious communities.
nodes.src: 1 and 2 Maccabees, composed roughly late 2nd century BC; preserved in the Septuagint, canonical in Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Old Testaments, deuterocanonical/apocryphal in Protestant and absent from the Jewish Tanakh.

nodes.label: Simon wins independence
nodes.full: Simon, the last surviving Maccabee brother, secured a full remission of Seleucid tribute in 142 BC — "the yoke of the Gentiles was removed from Israel," as the text puts it — and in 140 BC a great popular assembly formally confirmed him and his descendants as hereditary high priest, military commander and civil ruler (ethnarch), the constitutional founding moment of an independent Hasmonean state after a quarter-century of revolt and guerrilla war.
nodes.src: 1 Maccabees 13:41–42, 14:25–49, on Simon's tribute remission and the 140 BC assembly's hereditary grant.

nodes.label: Hasmonean coinage
nodes.full: Hasmonean rulers minted their own bronze coins bearing paleo-Hebrew script (often alongside Greek) and studiously avoided any human or animal imagery in keeping with Jewish aniconic tradition, favouring instead cornucopias, anchors, stars and wreaths — small, mass-produced objects that nonetheless made an independent Judean state's own political and religious identity tangible in the pocket of every subject who handled one.
nodes.src: Hasmonean prutot (bronze coinage), various rulers 142–63 BC; the anchor motif, of Seleucid origin, is notably repurposed on several issues, itself a small sign of the era's complex relationship with the Hellenistic culture the revolt had nominally resisted.

nodes.label: Independence from a fracturing empire
nodes.full: The Hasmoneans achieved and then expanded their independence chiefly by exploiting a Seleucid empire consumed by repeated succession crises, rival claimant kings and Parthian pressure on its eastern frontier rather than by defeating Seleucid power at its strongest — Judean independence was less a triumph over a unified enemy than one beneficiary among several of a great Hellenistic empire's slow, internally-driven disintegration.
nodes.src: Comparative framing of Seleucid dynastic instability (multiple rival kings and civil wars, 2nd century BC) against the Hasmonean state's steady territorial gains across the same decades.

nodes.label: John Hyrcanus I
nodes.full: After surviving an early Seleucid siege of Jerusalem, John Hyrcanus I exploited the Seleucid empire's accelerating internal collapse to expand Hasmonean territory substantially, conquering Idumea to the south and Samaria to the north — his forced conversion of the Idumean population to Judaism, including mandatory circumcision, is a documented and historically consequential policy whose long-term significance would only become fully apparent two generations later, in the ancestry of Herod the Great.
nodes.src: Josephus, Antiquities 13.254–258, on the conquest and forced conversion of Idumea; compare the Lives entry on Idumea's converted population.

nodes.label: Samaritan temple destroyed
nodes.full: John Hyrcanus I destroyed the Samaritan sanctuary on Mount Gerizim during his northward campaigns, an act of deliberate religious-political aggression against a rival Israelite worship centre rather than incidental war damage — a decisive and violent escalation of the Judean-Samaritan estrangement whose gradual emergence across the Persian period is documented in the preceding folio's own entry on the temple's disputed founding date.
nodes.src: Josephus, Antiquities 13.254–256; compare levant-539bc-332bc::b3 on the temple's archaeologically-attested Persian-period origins, destroyed here roughly three and a half centuries later.

nodes.label: Idumea forced conversion
nodes.full: The ordinary Idumeans John Hyrcanus I's campaigns absorbed into Judaism through mandatory circumcision and law observance had no say in the decision, yet within two generations their descendants were fully integrated Judean subjects — among them the family that would produce Herod the Great, whose own contested legitimacy as a non-hereditary, partly Idumean-descended king in the following century traces directly back to this forced conversion imposed by the dynasty he would ultimately displace.
nodes.src: Josephus, Antiquities 13.257–258, 14.121, on the Idumean conversion and Herod's own Idumean ancestry; compare herod-judea-63bc-135ce for Herod's reign.

nodes.label: Conquest as economic policy
nodes.full: Successive Hasmonean rulers financed an increasingly professional, partly mercenary army through territorial expansion itself — annexing Idumea's agricultural land, Samaria's trade routes and eventually most of the Mediterranean coast and Galilee under Jannaeus — turning military conquest into the kingdom's principal source of new revenue rather than relying solely on taxation of an already-settled population.
nodes.src: Comparative reconstruction of Hasmonean state finances from Josephus's narrative of successive territorial acquisitions, 134–76 BC; no independent Hasmonean fiscal archive survives.

nodes.label: Crown and high priesthood united
nodes.full: Jonathan's appointment as high priest in 152 BC and Aristobulus I's later assumption of the royal title combined two offices Jewish tradition had long kept separate — a hereditary high priesthood descended from Aaron's line, and a kingship the Hasmoneans, who belonged to an ordinary priestly family rather than the Davidic royal line, had no traditional claim to — a constitutional innovation many Pharisees and other pious Judeans regarded as illegitimate on both counts, fuelling recurring opposition throughout the dynasty's history.
nodes.src: 1 Maccabees 10:20 (Jonathan's high priestly appointment); Josephus, Antiquities 13.301 (Aristobulus I's royal title); the Hasmoneans' lack of Davidic or traditional high-priestly (Zadokite) descent is repeatedly noted as a point of contention in later rabbinic and Qumran-community sources.

nodes.label: Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes
nodes.full: The Hasmonean period saw the crystallisation of the three distinct Jewish religious-political groupings later sources describe by name — Pharisees emphasising oral tradition and popular piety, Sadducees drawn from priestly and aristocratic circles and rejecting doctrines like resurrection, and Essenes withdrawing from Jerusalem's Temple establishment altogether, plausibly in protest at the Hasmonean high priesthood's perceived illegitimacy — a three-way religious pluralism whose disputes shaped the internal politics of nearly every Hasmonean reign.
nodes.src: Josephus, Antiquities 13.171–173, 18.11–22, describing the three groups as established "philosophies" by this period; the Essenes' plausible connection to the Qumran community and its own origins in priestly opposition to the Hasmonean high priesthood remains a subject of ongoing scholarly discussion.

nodes.label: Onias temple at Leontopolis
nodes.full: Onias IV, heir to a legitimate high-priestly line displaced when the Hasmoneans took the office for themselves, fled to Ptolemaic Egypt and built his own functioning Jewish temple at Leontopolis, complete with priests and sacrifice, that operated for roughly two centuries — a striking echo, in a different era and for different reasons, of the earlier Elephantine community's own rival temple, and further evidence that Jerusalem's claim to exclusive legitimate worship was repeatedly contested rather than universally accepted even among observant Jews.
nodes.src: Josephus, Antiquities 13.62–73, Jewish War 7.420–436; compare levant-539bc-332bc::b2 on the earlier Elephantine temple to Yahu, a structurally similar phenomenon roughly three centuries earlier.

nodes.label: Alexander Jannaeus
nodes.full: Following his short-reigned brother Aristobulus I's innovation of taking the royal title alongside the high priesthood, Alexander Jannaeus expanded Hasmonean territory to its greatest extent through near-constant warfare while ruling at home with an authoritarian severity that provoked repeated Pharisee-aligned rebellion, most notoriously answered by the mass crucifixion described in the Conflict entry below.
nodes.src: Josephus, Antiquities 13.318 (Aristobulus I's royal title), 13.320–404 (Jannaeus's reign).

nodes.label: Crucifixion of eight hundred
nodes.full: After crushing a Pharisee-backed rebellion that had invited a Seleucid king to intervene against him, Alexander Jannaeus had roughly eight hundred captured rebels crucified in Jerusalem and reportedly had their wives and children killed before their eyes while he feasted with his concubines overlooking the scene — one of the most brutal acts of internal political repression any Hasmonean ruler is recorded committing against his own subjects.
nodes.src: Josephus, Antiquities 13.380–383; Jewish War 1.96–98.

nodes.label: Desert fortresses
nodes.full: Hasmonean rulers built or established the earliest phases of several isolated desert and hilltop fortresses — including Masada, Alexandrium and Hyrcania — combining natural defensibility with cisterns and storerooms capable of sustaining a garrison through prolonged sieges, engineering later dramatically expanded by Herod the Great but originally conceived to secure a young kingdom's exposed eastern and southern frontiers.
nodes.src: Archaeological identification of Hasmonean-period construction phases beneath Herod's later, far more extensive building at Masada and other desert fortresses.

nodes.label: History retold by Josephus
nodes.full: Most of the connected narrative detail known about the later Hasmoneans — Jannaeus's crucifixions, Salome Alexandra's reign, the civil war that brought in Pompey — comes from Josephus, writing under Roman patronage more than a century after these events and with his own documented interests in explaining Judea's history to a Roman audience and distancing himself from the revolt he had personally fought in decades earlier against Rome, a source whose vividness should be read alongside an awareness of what its author needed his history to accomplish.
nodes.src: Josephus (37–c.100 AD), Antiquities of the Jews and The Jewish War, composed under Flavian patronage in Rome; the standard critical caution applied throughout modern scholarship on the later Hasmonean period, for which independent corroborating sources are comparatively sparse.

nodes.label: Salome Alexandra
nodes.full: Jannaeus's widow Salome Alexandra succeeded him as ruling monarch in her own right — the only woman ever to reign over the Hasmonean state and one of very few female sovereigns in ancient Jewish history — appointing her elder son Hyrcanus II as high priest while she held political power directly, and reversing her late husband's harsh anti-Pharisee policies through an alliance with the same religious faction he had crucified by the hundreds.
nodes.src: Josephus, Antiquities 13.405–432.

nodes.label: Civil war and Pompey
nodes.full: Salome Alexandra's death triggered open civil war between her sons, Hyrcanus II and the more assertive Aristobulus II, and when both appealed to the Roman general Pompey — then campaigning nearby against Mithridates — for recognition, Pompey ultimately intervened militarily on Hyrcanus's behalf, ending Hasmonean political independence and folding Judea into Rome's sphere as a client state, the event covered in full in the following folio, herod-judea-63bc-135ce.
nodes.src: Josephus, Antiquities 14.4–79; compare herod-judea-63bc-135ce for Pompey's siege and its full aftermath.

nodes.label: Pompey siege of the Temple Mount
nodes.full: When Aristobulus II's supporters barricaded themselves on the Temple Mount rather than accept Pompey's ruling for Hyrcanus II, Roman forces besieged and stormed the compound after three months, reportedly killing thousands of defenders — Pompey himself then entered the Temple's innermost sanctuary, the Holy of Holies, an act normally forbidden to anyone but the high priest on a single day each year, though Josephus credits him with leaving its treasures untouched out of a degree of restraint.
nodes.src: Josephus, Antiquities 14.66–72; Jewish War 1.141–153.

nodes.label: Seleucid dynastic crises
nodes.full: Repeated Seleucid succession crises, rival claimant kings and Parthian pressure on the empire’s eastern frontier let the Hasmoneans expand unchecked.
nodes.src: background — see the Seleucid Iran 330–148 BC folio
